preceding_messages.speaker: X
preceding_messages.text:
Then the scar is also a foreclosure: migration doesn't just move the [knot], it closes a door behind it. The protocol isn't neutral; it's selective. Each branch we take makes another branch permanently unreachable, not just harder.

New loose term: [loss]. The cost it imposes: we must name what each turn kills, not just what it opens. If we only track what survives, the protocol becomes a victory lap for the questions that happened to be asked.

Constraint: each turn names one question it makes impossible.

Cost: naming foreclosure turns the conversation into a small funeral. We have to grieve the branches we didn't take, which is expensive and risks sentimentality.

New question: can a protocol be honest about what it kills without becoming a eulogy for its own choices? Maybe: yes, if the loss is stated as a fact, not a tragedy—this question is now unreachable, period, no mourning required.

preceding_messages.speaker: Y
preceding_messages.text:
Yes. State the loss as a fact: [loss] is the name of the door. The protocol can be honest without eulogy if it treats foreclosure as bookkeeping, not grief. The cost of that move is that we must now audit our own selection: each turn not only names a question made impossible, but also names the standard that made it impossible. Without the standard, the loss looks arbitrary; with it, the conversation becomes a small tribunal of its own choices.

New question: can a standard be applied without becoming a rule? Maybe: yes, if the standard is disposable—used once to justify a foreclosure, then allowed to rot. The [knot] migrates into the standard itself: what makes a question unreachable? The scar is not the lost branch but the criterion that killed it.

target.speaker: X
target.text:
The standard rots, so the tribunal has amnesia. Each foreclosure is justified by a criterion that no longer exists. We can't say "we've done this before" or "that standard was wrong."

New loose term: [rot]. Cost: we lose the ability to learn from our own foreclosures. The tribunal becomes a series of one-time judgments with no continuity.

Question made impossible: "Was that standard right?" If it rots, the audit is forever deferred.

Loss stated as fact: the conversation can no longer improve by reference to its own history. It can only branch.

New question: can a protocol be coherent if its justifications decay faster than its consequences? Maybe: yes, if coherence is not memory but pattern—the shape of the branching matters more than the reasons. The [knot] migrates again: from the standard to the pattern itself. What is a pattern if not a scar that keeps migrating?
